tagline.text: The green stone house where the Philippines' national hero was born and raised

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: Year-round (dry season Nov–Apr is easiest for travel)

children.text: A National Shrine that recreates, on its original site, the house where Filipino national hero Jose Rizal was born on

. Inside this Spanish colonial-era stone house, his childhood belongings and his family's living spaces have been re-created, and since there's no admission fee, it makes for an easy history outing just outside Manila.
Rizal Shrine Calamba is the house where Jose Rizal, the spiritual leader of the Philippine independence movement and the country's national hero, was born on

and spent his childhood. It stands at the center of Calamba's old town on the southern shore of Laguna Lake (Laguna de Bay), right next to San Juan Bautista Church, where Rizal was baptized. It's run by the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP) as the "Rizal Shrine Calamba" and is designated the highest-ranked category of National Shrine.

The original house was a two-story "bahay na bato" built over about two years by Rizal's father, Francisco Mercado. It's a classic mansion of the Spanish colonial-era Filipino elite, with a ground floor of stone and brick, an upper floor of solid wood, and sliding windows fitted with capiz shells. The Rizal family leased farmland owned by the Dominican order to grow sugarcane, but after a dispute over rent, Spanish authorities seized the house and evicted the family in
— an episode counted among the reasons Rizal came to write his critiques of the colonial system.
The house was destroyed during World War II, and its reconstruction was ordered by executive order of President Elpidio Quirino in

. Donations collected from students nationwide covered much of the rebuilding cost, and architect Juan Nakpil restored it using the period's original materials and construction methods, based on old photographs and testimony. It opened on Rizal's birthday,
, and in
its exterior was repainted the green it wears today, matching the meaning of Rizal's surname, "green fields."
It's modest in scale, and about
an hour

is enough to see it all. It suits travelers interested in Philippine history, expat families who want to tell their kids about a Filipino hero, and anyone looking for a stop on the way to Laguna's hot springs or Enchanted Kingdom. It's also a natural starting point for tracing Rizal's life from the beginning, continuing on to Rizal Park in Manila and Fort Santiago in Intramuros.

blocks.title: The room where Rizal was born

children.text: The bedroom where Rizal was born has been recreated in an inner room on the second floor. In this modest room with its four-poster bed and period furniture, imagine the hero's very first moments.
The ground-floor exhibit room displays Rizal's baptismal certificate, writings and drawings from his childhood, and family photographs. It offers a glimpse of the young Rizal's many talents.

blocks.title: A look at 19th-century wealthy household life

children.text: The spacious living room, dining room, study, kitchen, and the azotea, a rear terrace, all preserve the layout of a well-off Spanish-era Filipino household. Sunlight filtering through the capiz-shell windows adds to the atmosphere.

blocks.title: The statue of young Rizal and his dog

children.text: The garden holds a bronze statue of young Rizal standing with his dog, along with a traditional bahay kubo house. It's the best spot for a family photo.

blocks.title: San Juan Bautista Church, where he was baptized

children.text: The church right next to the shrine is where Rizal was baptized on
. The baptismal font used for his baptism still stands inside the church today.
In the plaza in front of city hall stands a
bronze statue of Rizal, erected in
for the 150th anniversary of his birth — its height a nod to the 22 languages Rizal is said to have mastered.
In the old town plaza stands "Kalambang," a giant jar sculpture said to be the origin of the city's name. It's within walking distance of the shrine.

The museum closes around
4 PM
and is closed on Mondays, so it's safer to visit the shrine earlier in the morning.
From Pasay Buendia, One Ayala in Makati, PITX, Cubao, and other terminals, take a bus bound for Calamba, Los Baños, Santa Cruz, or San Pablo and get off at "Calamba Crossing." It takes about
1 hour 30 minutes–2 hours 30 minutes
depending on traffic, for a one-way fare of about
From Calamba Crossing to the old town (Poblacion) where the shrine stands is about
2km
, reachable by jeepney or tricycle in
10–15 minutes
From Manila, take SLEX south for about
55km
and exit at Calamba. Without traffic it takes
1 hour–1 hour 30 minutes

, though SLEX gets heavily congested on weekend afternoons and holidays. The road in front of the shrine is narrow with little parking, so use the area around the church or a nearby paid parking lot. A Grab from Makati runs about
one way.
The shrine, the church, and Kalambang are all just a few minutes' walk from each other. You can charter a tricycle to the Rizal monument at city hall or the lakeside Baywalk for a round trip around
. Short trips within town start at about
Since it's an indoor museum, you can visit year-round regardless of weather. That said, if you plan to walk the garden and surrounding plaza too, the drier
November–April
season is more comfortable, and in
March–May
, when midday temperatures climb to
, a morning visit is recommended. During the
June–October
rainy season, afternoon showers are frequent, and low-lying roads along Laguna Lake can flood during typhoons.
Rizal's birthday,
June 19
, brings commemorative ceremonies and wreath-laying in Calamba, making it the busiest and most meaningful day around the shrine. Rizal Day, the national holiday marking his execution,
December 30
, also brings memorial events. Visiting routes may be restricted or hours changed on these dates, so check the museum's official page for the latest notices.
On weekday mornings during the school term, student groups on field trips are common. If you'd rather visit quietly, aim for a weekday afternoon or right after opening on a weekend morning.

A day trip from Manila is plenty, but if you're continuing a Laguna trip, staying in Calamba is also a good option. Business hotels around Calamba Crossing and the large malls run about

per night, while the Pansol area south of Calamba clusters hundreds of resorts, large and small, drawing on hot-spring water — many families rent a whole private-pool villa. Weekend rates run considerably higher than weekdays, so compare in advance.

The old town around the shrine has simple Filipino restaurants and cafes, and franchise restaurants cluster around Calamba Crossing and the malls. Since you're in Laguna, try or buy as gifts the specialties of neighboring Los Baños: buko pie, espasol (a cylindrical rice-flour sweet), and kesong puti, Laguna's soft white cheese. At the Pansol hot-spring resorts, enjoying a Filipino-style family meal of grilled meat and seafood after a swim is a typical local weekend scene.
The museum generally operates Tuesday through Sunday, around
9 AM to 4 PM
, and is closed Mondays and some public holidays. Check the NHCP museum's official page for hours before you visit.
Admission is free, but you'll sign a guestbook on entry. There's a donation box for upkeep, so a small contribution is welcome.
Groups of 10 or more can request a guided tour in advance through the museum.
Flash photography and touching the exhibits are prohibited indoors. Follow the on-site staff's guidance on what photography is allowed.
The church and shrine are places of reverence, so modest dress is better than sleeveless tops or short shorts.
Knowing the plots of Rizal's novels "Noli Me Tangere" and "El Filibusterismo" beforehand makes the exhibits much more interesting.
SLEX gets very congested toward Manila on weekend afternoons. Time your return trip for before 3 PM or late in the evening.
The shrine is closed on Mondays. It may also close temporarily for holidays like Rizal Day or for renovations, so check the latest notices before you set out.
Today's house is a faithful reconstruction of the original. Much of the furniture on display was sourced to match the period style, and not all of it consists of actual Rizal family heirlooms.
The streets of the old town are narrow, with heavy car and tricycle traffic and tight sidewalks. Hold your child's hand firmly if you're traveling with kids.
The Calamba Crossing bus stop and the area around the malls are always busy. Keep your phone and wallet in front of you.
